content:
The objection says that honour killings cluster in Muslim societies, that the laws of Muslim countries excuse them, and that the Prophet himself praised a man's jealousy. The killings are real, and they are crimes under the law the critic blames.[1]

The seven answers separate what the Quran and the law require from what custom does, and from penal codes that came from Europe.

An accusation of adultery needs four witnesses, and those who accuse without them are flogged (24:4). A husband who has no witnesses swears the li'ān oath, his wife may swear in reply, and the marriage ends. No one is killed (24:6-9).[2]

The Quran forbids taking a life except by right (17:33), and it counts one unjust killing as the killing of all humanity (5:32).[2]

Sa'd asked whether, finding a man with his wife, he must wait to bring four witnesses. The Prophet said yes.

When Sa'd said that he would strike with the sword, the Prophet spoke of Sa'd's jealousy and said that God is more jealous still. He gave no permission (Sahih Muslim 1498).[3]

On the rule the answer was plain: wait for the witnesses. The Prophet refused the sword.[3]

The ruling reported from 'Ali is that a man who kills an adulterer is liable to retaliation unless he brings proof.[4]

Killers have tried to hide behind the law's mercy. Where heirs may pardon, a family that kills its own daughter can try to pardon itself. Muslim lawmakers and muftis answered that abuse in the name of the sharia, as the next answer shows.[4][5]

Pakistan's Criminal Law (Amendment) (Offences in the Name or Pretext of Honour) Act 2016 made a pardon by the heirs ineffective against a life sentence for such a killing.[5]

Jordan amended Article 340 of its penal code in 2001, from exemption to a reduced penalty. In 2017 it barred the "fit of fury" mitigation for crimes against women.

The article descends from French penal law. Jordan's official fatwa department ruled in December 2016 that killing a relative to cleanse the family honour is an act against the sharia.[6]

The UN Population Fund's report of 2000 said that "perhaps as many as 5,000" women and girls are killed each year in the name of honour. It also noted that Muslim religious leaders condemn the practice.[7]

The figure is old and its method was not published. Later estimates range up to 20,000, and researchers note that the evidence behind all of them is unclear.[8]

Honour killing is documented among Hindu and Sikh families in India. Brazil's courts allowed a defence of "legitimate defence of honour" until the Supreme Federal Court barred it in 2021. Italy reduced the penalty for delitto d'onore until 1981.[8]

The Quran's procedure makes private killing a crime, the Prophet refused the sword, and Muslim states and muftis have shut the door on killers who sought cover in the law. The practice is a crime of custom that the sharia condemns.

The related articles are 6 facts about women in Islamic law and when a father says "this is Islam". Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Human Rights Watch, Honoring the Killers: Justice Denied for "Honor" Crimes in Jordan (2004).
  2. Quran 24:2-9, 17:33, 5:32.
  3. Sahih Muslim 1498; the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  4. Malik, al-Muwatta', the book of judgements; Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni, the book of injuries; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1400; the hadith texts are on searchtruth.com.
  5. Pakistan, Act XLIII of 2016 (ILO NATLEX); Sohail Akbar Warraich, "'Honour Killings' and the Law in Pakistan", in Lynn Welchman and Sara Hossain (eds.), 'Honour': Crimes, Paradigms and Violence against Women (London: Zed, 2005), 78-110.
  6. UN ESCWA, Jordan: Gender Justice and the Law (2018); The National, 3 December 2016, on the fatwa of 1 December 2016.
  7. UNFPA, The State of World Population 2000, chapter 3.
  8. Tanya D'Lima, Jennifer L. Solotaroff and Rohini P. Pande, "For the Sake of Family and Tradition: Honour Killings in India and Pakistan", ANTYAJAA 5/1 (2020): 22-39; Italy, Law 442 of 1981; Brazil, Supreme Federal Court, ADPF 779 (2021).
